newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN set to mediate in Cambodian crisis.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN set to mediate in Cambodian crisis.

text.p: ASEAN was preparing fresh proposals on Thursday to Cambodian strongman Hun Sen in an attempt to mediate in the conflict in his country, and U.S. Secretary of State Madeline Albright urged him to cooperate.

Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas, who has been involved in brokering Cambodian diplomacy for years, said he and two other Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) ministers discussed the ideas with Cambodian Foreign Minister Ung Huot on Wednesday.
"The three ministers will try to pick up the thread where we left it and continue our efforts," he told Reuters on Thursday.

Alatas and two other members of an ASEAN delegation -- Thai Foreign Minister Prachaub Chaiyasan and Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon -- met Hun Sen last weekend in Phnom Penh offering their mediation services.

Hun Sen rejected the offer out of hand then, saying foreigners should stay out of Cambodia's business. But in an apparent change of heart, his foreign minister, Ung Huot, told ASEAN that Hun Sen was now prepared to accept the regional group's intervention.
Alatas said the foreign ministers did not have time to get into substantive issues at the meeting on Wednesday but "we have exchanged some views and now we are starting".

ASEAN on Thursday began its annual two-day meeting with two new members -- Burma and Laos -- in the lineup. Cambodia was also supposed to be inducted as a new member on Wednesday. But ASEAN postponed its entry due to the political turmoil there.
ASEAN considers Hun Sen's violent overthrow of First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh on July 5-6 to be against the principles of the 1991 Paris Peace Accords it helped create.
Alatas told reporters late on Wednesday it was premature to predict Hun Sen's reaction to the proposals, but added:
"We hope to make progress and of course, as quickly as possible, as time is running out. I don't know how they will respond."

One Southeast Asian diplomat said Ung Huot was possibly trying to sway ASEAN ministers into speedily admitting Cambodia to the grouping by accepting the mediation offer. "Hun Sen probably told him to say whatever he had to say," he said.

A senior ASEAN source said it was highly unlikely Cambodia would be admitted in the near future. He said it was more likely to happen during an annual ASEAN summit in December if the situation in Cambodia was straightened out, "although in politics anything can happen".
ASEAN, celebrating its 30th year, now comprises Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, Vietnam, the Philippines, Brunei, Burma and Laos.
In Los Angeles on Wednesday, Albright pledged that the United States would do all it could to see that Hun Sen made good on promises to accept mediation.
She also challenged ASEAN to play a greater role in Burma, saying that by admitting Burma as a member this year, "Burma's problems now become ASEAN's problems."
"The United States will use its leverage and do all we can in partnership with others to see that Hun Sen's words are translated into concrete action," Albright said.
"This will be one of our primary goals at the (ASEAN) meetings this weekend in Kuala Lumpur," she said.
Albright, along with foreign ministers from other Western and Asian powers, will attend the ASEAN Regional Forum, the premier vehicle for political and security talks in Asia.
